claim: CH503 is the anti-aphrodisiac pheromone (3R,11Z,19Z)-3-acetoxy-11,19-octacosadien-1-ol.
source: Here, we describe a male-specific gustatory circuit in Drosophila that underlies the detection of the anti-aphrodisiac pheromone (3R,11Z,19Z)-3-acetoxy-11,19-octacosadien-1-ol (CH503).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines CH503 as (3R,11Z,19Z)-3-acetoxy-11,19-octacosadien-1-ol and identifies it as an anti-aphrodisiac pheromone.

claim: Gr68a-expressing neurons on the forelegs of male flies exhibit a sexually dimorphic physiological response to CH503.
source: Using behavioral analysis, genetic manipulation, and live calcium imaging, we show that Gr68a-expressing neurons on the forelegs of male flies exhibit a sexually dimorphic physiological response to the pheromone and relay information to the central brain via peptidergic neurons.
evidence: The abstract states that behavioral analysis, genetic manipulation, and live calcium imaging were used to demonstrate this sexually dimorphic response.

claim: Gr68a-expressing neurons relay information to the central brain via peptidergic neurons.
source: Using behavioral analysis, genetic manipulation, and live calcium imaging, we show that Gr68a-expressing neurons on the forelegs of male flies exhibit a sexually dimorphic physiological response to the pheromone and relay information to the central brain via peptidergic neurons.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that information is relayed to the central brain via peptidergic neurons.

claim: The release of tachykinin from 8 to 10 cells within the subesophageal zone is required for CH503-triggered courtship suppression.
source: The release of tachykinin from 8 to 10 cells within the subesophageal zone is required for the pheromone-triggered courtship suppression.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that tachykinin release from 8-10 cells in the SEZ is required for courtship suppression.

claim: CH503 is transferred from males to females during mating.
source: CH503 is transferred from males to females during mating and inhibits courtship from other males (Yew et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yew et al., 2009 as the source for this claim.

claim: CH503 inhibits courtship from other males after being transferred to females.
source: CH503 is transferred from males to females during mating and inhibits courtship from other males (Yew et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yew et al., 2009 as the source for this claim.

claim: CH503 functions as a potent suppressor of male courtship behavior in other drosophilids.
source: The pheromone also functions as a potent suppressor of male courtship behavior in other drosophilids (Ng et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ng et al., 2014 as the source for this claim.

claim: A dose of 167 ng/fly of CH503 was sufficient to suppress courtship in approximately 50% of behavioral trials.
source: A dose of 167 ng/fly was sufficient to suppress courtship in approximately 50% of the behavioral trials (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data showing dose-dependent courtship suppression, with Figure 1B providing visual evidence.

claim: The latency to courtship initiation was similar across all CH503 doses, ranging from 350 to 400 s.
source: The latency to courtship initiation (as measured by the first instance of wing vibration) was similar across all doses, ranging from 350 to 400 s (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data on latency to courtship initiation, with Figure 1C providing visual evidence.

claim: CH503 significantly suppressed overall courtship vigor.
source: However, the overall courtship vigor was significantly suppressed by the pheromone (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data showing suppression of courtship vigor, with Figure 1D providing visual evidence.

claim: CH503 inhibits later stages of the courtship sequence and sustained courtship behavior.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that CH503 inhibits later stages of the courtship sequence and sustained courtship behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on latency and courtship vigor.

claim: CH503 has low volatility.
source: CH503 has low volatility and inhibits courtship only when detected on female cuticles.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data showing that CH503 does not inhibit courtship when separated from females, with Figure 1E providing visual evidence.

claim: CH503 inhibits courtship only when detected on female cuticles.
source: CH503 has low volatility and inhibits courtship only when detected on female cuticles. The absence of female cuticular hydrocarbons in oenocyte-less (oe-) flies also did not affect CH503-induced courtship suppression.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data showing that CH503 must be on female cuticles to inhibit courtship, with Figure 1E providing visual evidence.

claim: The absence of female cuticular hydrocarbons in oenocyte-less flies did not affect CH503-induced courtship suppression.
source: The absence of female cuticular hydrocarbons in oenocyte-less (oe-) flies also did not affect CH503-induced courtship suppression.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data using oenocyte-less flies, with Figure 1E providing visual evidence.

claim: Female-specific pheromones synthesized in the oenocytes do not mediate the detection of CH503.
source: In sum, these results indicate that female-specific pheromones synthesized in the oenocytes do not mediate the detection of CH503.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data using oenocyte-less flies.

claim: CH503 is effective as an anti-aphrodisiac only when placed on the cuticular surface of females.
source: Furthermore, CH503 is effective as an anti-aphrodisiac only when placed on the cuticular surface of females, indicating that sensory cues other than cuticular lipids are required.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on CH503 placement.

claim: Sensory cues other than cuticular lipids are required for CH503 to be effective.
source: Furthermore, CH503 is effective as an anti-aphrodisiac only when placed on the cuticular surface of females, indicating that sensory cues other than cuticular lipids are required.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Exposure of male forelegs to 0.5–2.0 µg of CH503 together with 4% sucrose reduced the frequency of the proboscis extension reflex (PER).
source: Exposure of the forelegs to 0.5–2.0 µg of CH503 together with 4% sucrose reduced the frequency of the PER (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from PER assays, with Figure 2A providing visual evidence.

claim: Caffeine, a bitter stimulus, suppressed the PER in males.
source: Similarly, caffeine, a bitter stimulus, also suppressed the PER.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from PER assays.

claim: Females did not exhibit a change in the PER when exposed to CH503.
source: In contrast, females did not exhibit a change in the PER when exposed to CH503, indicating that either the pheromone was not detected or that it does not carry a negative valence for females (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from PER assays with females, with Figure 2—figure supplement 1 providing visual evidence.

claim: Or83b-defective flies still suppressed courtship in the presence of CH503.
source: However, Or83b-defective flies still suppressed courtship in the presence of CH503 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data using Or83b mutants, with Figure 2B providing visual evidence.

claim: Voila1 mutants, which exhibit gustatory defects, continued to court CH503-perfumed females.
source: In contrast, Voila1 mutants, which exhibit gustatory defects (Balakireva et al., 1998), continued to court CH503-perfumed females (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data using Voila1 mutants, with Figure 2B providing visual evidence and citation to Balakireva et al., 1998.

claim: CH503 is perceived as an aversive tastant by males and not females.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that CH503 is perceived as an aversive tastant by males and not females and is detected by gustatory receptors on the foreleg.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PER assay data and mutant studies.

claim: CH503 is detected by gustatory receptors on the foreleg.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that CH503 is perceived as an aversive tastant by males and not females and is detected by gustatory receptors on the foreleg.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PER assay data and mutant studies.

claim: Males in which the Gr68a-encoding gene was transcriptionally silenced continued to court females in the presence of (S, Z, Z)-CH503.
source: However, males in which the Gr68a-encoding gene was transcriptionally silenced continued to court females in the presence of (S, Z, Z)-CH503 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data using Gr68a RNAi, with Figure 2B providing visual evidence.

claim: ΔGr68a mutants displayed robust courtship behavior in the presence of CH503-perfumed females.
source: ΔGr68 mutants displayed robust courtship behavior in the presence of CH503-perfumed females (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data using ΔGr68a mutants, with Figure 2C providing visual evidence.

claim: The sensitivity to CH503 was restored upon re-introduction of the Gr68a-encoding gene.
source: Importantly, the sensitivity to CH503 was restored upon re-introduction of the Gr68a-encoding gene (Gr68aRes; Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data using Gr68a rescue lines, with Figure 2C providing visual evidence.

claim: CG6024 expression was not significantly changed in either mutant or rescue lines.
source: However, CG6024 expression was not significantly changed in either mutant or rescue lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data showing no change in CG6024 expression, with Figure 2—figure supplement 3 providing visual evidence.

claim: Activation of Gr68a neurons using dTrpA1 resulted in a slight but non-significant suppression in courtship behavior at 29°C compared with 19°C.
source: In the presence of unperfumed female targets, a slight but non-significant suppression in courtship behavior was observed at the activation temperature of 29°C compared with the inactive condition at 19°C (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data using dTrpA1, with Figure 2C providing visual evidence.

claim: Activation of Gr68a neurons is not sufficient to suppress courtship.
source: Thus, activation of Gr68a neurons is not sufficient to suppress courtship, possibly due to conflicting signals resulting from mutual activation of mechanosensory and chemosensory neurons (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dTrpA1 experimental data.

claim: A sexually dimorphic GFP expression pattern was observed in the chemosensory neurons of gustatory bristles found in male forelegs.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Bray and Amrein, 2003; Ejima and Griffith, 2008; Ling et al., 2014), a sexually dimorphic GFP expression pattern was observed in the chemosensory neurons of gustatory bristles found in male forelegs (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging data showing sexually dimorphic expression, with Figure 3A providing visual evidence and citations to previous reports.

claim: Each of the male tarsal segments exhibited more labeled neurons than females.
source: Each of the male tarsal segments exhibited more labeled neurons than females (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports cell counting data, with Table 1 providing quantitative evidence.

claim: Labeled non-neuronal cells were observed only in male legs.
source: Labeled non-neuronal cells (distinguished by larger, irregularly shaped membranes lacking projections) were also observed but only in male legs (Figure 3A; Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging and cell counting data, with Figure 3A and Table 1 providing visual and quantitative evidence.

claim: Knockdown of Gr68a expression using the pan-neuronal elav-Gal4 driver resulted in a loss of sensitivity to CH503.
source: Notably, knockdown of Gr68a expression using the pan-neuronal elav-Gal4 driver resulted in a loss of sensitivity to CH503 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data using elav-Gal4 to drive Gr68a RNAi, with Figure 2B providing visual evidence.

claim: Neuronally expressed Gr68a receptors are important for CH503 detection.
source: The results recapitulate the phenotype observed with Gr68a-Gal4 and indicate that neuronally expressed receptors are important for CH503 detection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the elav-Gal4 experimental data.

claim: At a dose of 500 ng of (R, Z, Z)-CH503, 6 of 9 cells in segments T2–4 showed significant responses compared to the control solvent.
source: At this dose, 6 of 9 cells in segments T2–4 showed significant responses compared to the control solvent, ranging from ΔF/F 0.34 ± 0.05 to 1.39 ± 0.46 (mean ± SEM).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data showing cellular responses to CH503.

claim: At a dose of 50 ng, only 1 cell (T4, Cell a) showed a significant signal increase, with an average ΔF/F of 1.52 ± 0.37.
source: At a dose of 50 ng, only 1 cell (T4, Cell a) showed a significant signal increase, with an average ΔF/F of 1.52 ± 0.37.
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data showing cellular responses to CH503.

claim: Gr68a-neurons exhibited two general patterns of responses: a phasic response and a tonic response.
source: Gr68-neurons exhibited two general patterns of responses: more commonly, a phasic response is observed where maximum fluorescent intensity occurred immediately after the addition of the pheromone and was followed by a gradual decline to baseline levels after 6 s. A tonic response is also seen where fluorescence gradually increased and peaked after approximately 120 s (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data showing different response patterns, with Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Video 1 providing visual evidence.

claim: Stimulation of Gr68a-expressing neurons with a synthetic CH503 analog containing two triple bonds did not elicit a change in fluorescent signal.
source: Stimulation of Gr68a-expressing neurons with a synthetic CH503 analog containing two triple bonds did not elicit a change in fluorescent signal (Figure 3B), consistent with previous observations that the analog is behaviorally inert (Shikichi et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data using a CH503 analog, with Figure 3B providing visual evidence and citation to Shikichi et al., 2013.

claim: CH503 failed to evoke a physiological response when Gr68a expression was either reduced using RNAi or eliminated in ΔGr68a mutants.
source: Additionally, CH503 failed to evoke a physiological response when Gr68a expression was either reduced using RNAi or eliminated in ΔGr68a mutants (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data using Gr68a RNAi and mutants, with Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 providing visual evidence.

claim: In females, the responses to CH503 from the forelegs were indistinguishable from that of the solvent control.
source: In females, the responses to the pheromone from the forelegs were indistinguishable from that of the solvent control (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data from female flies, with Figure 3D providing visual evidence.

claim: The double-bonds in the carbon backbone of the CH503 molecule are an essential structural feature for pheromone activity.
source: Taken together, direct measurement of neural response in Gr68a-expressing neurons reveals robust functional activation by CH503 in males only. Moreover, the double-bonds in the carbon backbone of the CH503 molecule are an essential structural feature for pheromone activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the calcium imaging data using CH503 analogs.

claim: In the male proboscis, CH503 activated approximately 8 of 14 ppk23 neurons.
source: In the male proboscis, CH503 activated approximately 8 of 14 neurons while none of the female ppk23 neurons responded (Figure 3—figure supplement 4; Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data from ppk23 neurons, with Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Video 2 providing visual evidence.

claim: None of the female ppk23 neurons responded to CH503.
source: In the male proboscis, CH503 activated approximately 8 of 14 neurons while none of the female ppk23 neurons responded (Figure 3—figure supplement 4; Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data from ppk23 neurons, with Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Video 2 providing visual evidence.

claim: Males with ppk23 expression silenced using RNAi continued to respond to CH503 though the courtship suppression effect is partially mitigated.
source: Males continued to respond to CH503 though the courtship suppression effect is partially mitigated compared to other gustatory receptors (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using ppk23 RNAi, with Figure 2B providing visual evidence.

claim: Knockdown of ppk25 resulted in a partially reduced sensitivity to CH503.
source: Knockdown of a second member of the ppk family, ppk25, also resulted in a partially reduced sensitivity to CH503 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using ppk25 RNAi, with Figure 2B providing visual evidence.

claim: The responses of ppk-23/25-expressing neurons by themselves are not the primary sensory pathway and do not appear to be necessary for courtship suppression to occur.
source: While these results do not eliminate the possibility that ppk-23/25-expressing neurons contribute to CH503 detection, both the physiological and behavioral data indicate that the responses of the cells by themselves are not the primary sensory pathway and do not appear to be necessary for courtship suppression to occur.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ppk23/25 behavioral and physiological data.

claim: Gr68a-Gal4-labeled neurons send axonal projections to each of the six thoracico-abdominal (TAG) neuromeres and extend into the SEZ and the AMMC.
source: The Gr68a-Gal4-labeled neurons send axonal projections to each of the six thoracico-abdominal (TAG) neuromeres and extend into the SEZ and the antennal mechanosensory and motor center (AMMC) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging data showing projection patterns, with Figure 4A providing visual evidence.

claim: Suppression of neural activity using the c929-Gal4 line resulted in a marked decrease in sensitivity to CH503.
source: Interestingly, suppression of neural activity using the c929-Gal4 line resulted in a marked decrease in sensitivity to CH503 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using c929-Gal4, with Figure 4B providing visual evidence.

claim: c929-labeled processes in the thoracic ganglia do not appear to contribute to the behavioral response to CH503.
source: We partially limited c929-Gal4 expression by suppressing Gal4 activity in the ventral nerve cord with the repressor tsh-Gal80 and observed that sensitivity to CH503 was not restored (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Hence, c929-labeled processes in the thoracic ganglia do not appear to contribute to the behavioral response to CH503.
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using tsh-Gal80 to restrict c929-Gal4 expression, with Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 providing visual evidence.

claim: Genetic ablation or suppression of neural activity in neuropeptide F (NPF) circuits reduced sensitivity to CH503.
source: However, genetic ablation or suppression of neural activity in two neuropeptidergic circuits, neuropeptide F (NPF) and tachykinin (TK), reduced sensitivity to CH503 (Figure 4C; Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using NPF circuit manipulations, with Figure 4C providing visual evidence.

claim: Genetic ablation or suppression of neural activity in tachykinin (TK) circuits reduced sensitivity to CH503.
source: However, genetic ablation or suppression of neural activity in two neuropeptidergic circuits, neuropeptide F (NPF) and tachykinin (TK), reduced sensitivity to CH503 (Figure 4C; Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using TK circuit manipulations, with Figure 5A providing visual evidence.

claim: Gr68a synaptic terminals and NPF-positive processes are closely apposed to each other in the SEZ.
source: Anatomical analysis revealed that Gr68a synaptic terminals and NPF-positive processes are closely apposed to each other in the SEZ, implicating NPF-expressing circuits as a putative second order relay to the central brain (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging data showing anatomical proximity, with Figure 4D providing visual evidence.

claim: Silencing NPF expression using c929-Gal4 or the pan-neural driver elav-Gal4 was ineffective at changing the male inhibitory courtship response.
source: Notably, silencing NPF expression using c929-Gal4 or the pan-neural driver elav-Gal4 (which caused a 5.3-fold decrease in transcript level, Figure 4—figure supplement 4) was ineffective at changing the male inhibitory courtship response (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using NPF RNAi, with Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4 providing visual evidence.

claim: The NPF peptide itself is not likely to be essential for mediating CH503-related behavior.
source: These findings indicate that the NPF peptide itself is not likely to be essential for mediating CH503-related behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the NPF RNAi behavioral data.

claim: Silencing of the neuronal circuits associated with the NPF receptor, NPFR, did not change the response to CH503.
source: Consistent with this observation, silencing of the neuronal circuits associated with the NPF receptor, NPFR, also did not change the response to CH503 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using NPFR circuit manipulations, with Figure 4—figure supplement 1 providing visual evidence.

claim: Genetic excision of the TK gene caused a striking loss of sensitivity to CH503.
source: Genetic excision of the TK gene also caused a striking loss of sensitivity to CH503 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using TK deletion mutants, with Figure 5A providing visual evidence.

claim: The phenotype of TK mutants was rescued upon ectopic expression of TK in the mutant background.
source: The phenotype was rescued upon ectopic expression of TK in the mutant background (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using TK rescue lines, with Figure 5A providing visual evidence.

claim: The product of the TK gene is necessary for mediating the behavioral actions induced by CH503.
source: Thus, in contrast to our findings with the NPF peptide, the product of the TK gene is necessary for mediating the behavioral actions induced by CH503.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TK mutant and rescue data.

claim: Positive TK staining is evident in the SEZ and AMMC and is positioned closely to Gr68a-Gal4-labeled terminals.
source: Positive TK staining is evident in the SEZ and AMMC and is positioned closely to Gr68a-Gal4-labeled terminals (Figure 5B,C,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunohistochemistry data showing TK and Gr68a proximity, with Figure 5B, C, and E providing visual evidence.

claim: Positive GRASP-GFP staining was apparent in the SEZ (6 out of 10 brains) and the AMMC (9 out of 10 brains), indicating connectivity between Gr68a and TK neurons.
source: Positive GRASP-GFP staining was apparent in the SEZ (Figure 5D; 6 out of 10 brains) and the AMMC (Figure 5F; 9 out of 10 brains), indicating connectivity.
evidence: The manuscript reports GRASP data showing synaptic connectivity, with Figure 5D and F providing visual evidence.

claim: Silencing TK expression only within NPF-Gal4 populations resulted in a reduced response to CH503.
source: Indeed, silencing TK expression only within either of these Gal4-defined populations resulted in a reduced response to CH503, with male courtship levels indistinguishable from those of the solvent-perfumed fly (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using TK RNAi in NPF-Gal4 circuits, with Figure 6A providing visual evidence.

claim: Silencing TK expression only within c929-Gal4 populations resulted in a reduced response to CH503.
source: Indeed, silencing TK expression only within either of these Gal4-defined populations resulted in a reduced response to CH503, with male courtship levels indistinguishable from those of the solvent-perfumed fly (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using TK RNAi in c929-Gal4 circuits, with Figure 6C providing visual evidence.

claim: Conditional suppression of TK only from late pupal stage onwards produced the same phenotype as constitutive suppression.
source: Conditional suppression of TK only from late pupal stage onwards (using temperature-sensitive Gal80) also produced the same phenotype, indicating that loss of CH503 sensitivity from TK knockdown is not due to non-specific developmental effects (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using temperature-sensitive Gal80, with Figure 6A providing visual evidence.

claim: Co-expression of NPF and TK2-Gal4 is evident in 7 cells in the anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum.
source: Co-expression in 7 cells (designated NPF-TK cells) was evident in the anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunohistochemistry data showing co-expression, with Figure 6B providing visual evidence.

claim: Rescuing TK expression only within the NPF circuit did not restore the courtship suppression response.
source: First, on a TK mutant background, rescuing TK expression only within the NPF circuit did not restore the courtship suppression response (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using TK rescue in NPF circuits, with Figure 6A providing visual evidence.

claim: The four NPF-TK cells in the protocerebrum are not sufficient for mediating courtship suppression.
source: However, two lines of evidence indicate that these 4 cells are not sufficient for mediating courtship suppression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the NPF-TK rescue data and TK3-Gal4 data.

claim: Co-expression of c929-Gal4 and TK is evident in 10 cells in the SEZ.
source: In wild-type flies, co-expression is evident in 10 cells in the SEZ, designated as c929-TK cells (Figure 6D,D′).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunohistochemistry data showing co-expression, with Figure 6D and D′ providing visual evidence.

claim: Rescue of TK expression only in the 10 c929-TK cells restored the pheromone-response behavior in the ΔTK2 and ΔTK1/2 transheterozygote mutant background.
source: Rescue of TK expression only in these 10 cells restored the pheromone-response behavior in the ΔTK2 and ΔTK1/2 transheterozygote mutant background (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data using TK rescue in c929-Gal4 circuits, with Figure 6C providing visual evidence.

claim: TK release from a cluster of 8–10 cells within the SEZ is necessary to mediate the response to the gustatory pheromone CH503.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that TK release from a cluster of 8–10 cells within the SEZ is necessary to mediate the response to the gustatory pheromone CH503.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TK rescue and co-expression data.

claim: NPF-Gal4 and TK expression overlap in a small population of cells in the SEZ and protocerebrum.
source: In addition, NPF-Gal4 and TK expression overlap in a small population of cells in the SEZ and protocerebrum.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the triple labeling data.

claim: Gr68a has a dual sensory role in courtship initiation, detecting both motion-related cues and the male sex pheromone CH503.
source: The dual sensory role of Gr68a is consistent with its expression pattern in males in separate mechanosensory and gustatory neuron populations (Ejima and Griffith, 2008) and afferent projections to the SEZ and AMMC, a relay center for auditory information.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the expression pattern and projection data, with citation to Ejima and Griffith, 2008.

claim: Excitatory mechanosensory information is integrated with inhibitory CH503 detection via Gr68a neurons.
source: Thus, males' inability to detect motion rather than female pheromones may underlie the previously reported Gr68a-related courtship initiation defects. Taken together with the results of our current study, we propose that excitatory mechanosensory information is integrated with inhibitory CH503 detection via Gr68a neurons and both types of sensory cues shape the decision to initiate and sustain courtship.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Simultaneous activation of both courtship-promoting and suppressing channels likely resulted in an overall null response in dTrpA1 experiments.
source: This model is consistent with our findings that activation of Gr68a-neurons using TrpA1 did not promote courtship suppression. Simultaneous activation of both courtship-promoting and suppressing channels likely resulted in an overall null response.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the dTrpA1 experimental results.

claim: The amount of CH503 transferred to females during courtship is approximately 60–100 ng based on semi-quantitative mass spectral analysis.
source: However, the quantity that is transferred to the female during courtship is approximately 60–100 ng based on semi-quantitative mass spectral analysis of recently mated females.
evidence: The manuscript reports mass spectrometry data on CH503 transfer.

claim: D. melanogaster males have adapted to become less sensitive to CH503 to circumvent the courtship inhibitory response.
source: Additionally, recent findings indicate that male D. melanogaster have adapted to become less sensitive to CH503 to circumvent the courtship inhibitory response (Ng et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ng et al., 2014 as the source for this claim.

claim: Approximately 80 ng of CH503 is sufficient to inhibit male courtship in other non-CH503 producing drosophilid species.
source: While ∼80 ng is sufficient to inhibit male courtship in other non-CH503 producing drosophilid species, D. melanogaster males (and males of other species that express CH503) have become less sensitive to the molecule in order to avoid chemical coercion from other males (Ng et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ng et al., 2014 as the source for this claim.

claim: Gr68a neurons co-localize with fruitless.
source: Since ppk23 neurons co-localize with fruitless (Thistle et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2012), a master gene that regulates many aspects of courtship behavior (Yamamoto and Koganezawa, 2013), whereas Gr68a neurons do not (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), it is clear that Gr68a and ppk23 expression will also be in distinct populations of neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging data showing lack of co-localization, with Figure 3—figure supplement 6 providing visual evidence and citations to Thistle et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2012; and Yamamoto and Koganezawa, 2013.

claim: ppk23 neurons function as general detectors for a subset of chemosensory cues rather than encode information about valence.
source: Based on previous observations that ppk23 neurons respond to both attractive and aversive sex pheromones, we speculate that they function as general detectors for a subset of chemosensory cues rather than encode information about valence.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on previous observations.

claim: The AMMC was recently identified as a higher-order processing target for gustatory projection neurons from the SEZ which convey sweet information.
source: Intriguingly, the AMMC was recently identified as a higher-order processing target for gustatory projection neurons from the SEZ which convey sweet information (Kain and Dahanukar, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kain and Dahanukar, 2015 as the source for this claim.

claim: The TK circuitry serves as a point of convergence for multiple, opposing physiological drives which underlie an animal's decision to mate.
source: In this regard, the TK circuitry serves as a point of convergence for multiple, opposing physiological drives which underlie an animal's decision to mate (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TK circuit data, with Figure 7 providing a visual model.

claim: TK has been implicated in lipid metabolism.
source: TK has been implicated in numerous systemic functions including lipid metabolism (Song et al., 2014), stress resistance (Kahsai et al., 2010), and modulation of aggression levels (Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Song et al., 2014 as the source for this claim.

claim: TK has been implicated in stress resistance.
source: TK has been implicated in numerous systemic functions including lipid metabolism (Song et al., 2014), stress resistance (Kahsai et al., 2010), and modulation of aggression levels (Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kahsai et al., 2010 as the source for this claim.

claim: TK has been implicated in modulation of aggression levels.
source: TK has been implicated in numerous systemic functions including lipid metabolism (Song et al., 2014), stress resistance (Kahsai et al., 2010), and modulation of aggression levels (Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Asahina et al., 2014 as the source for this claim.

claim: The mammalian homolog of TK, Substance P, controls sexual behavior, stress responses, appetite, and aggression.
source: In addition, the mammalian homolog Substance P controls sexual behavior, stress responses, appetite, and aggression (Argiolas and Melis, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites Argiolas and Melis, 2013 as the source for this claim.

claim: The choice to fight or court is modulated by TK release which is, in part, regulated by external stimuli such as pheromones.
source: The convergence of aggression and sex within a common neural pathway alludes to the possibility that the choice to fight or court is modulated by TK release which is, in part, regulated by external stimuli such as pheromones.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the TK circuit data.

claim: The c929-TK cells identified in this study were shown previously to be involved in water conservation in response to desiccation.
source: Interestingly, the c929-TK cells identified in this study were shown previously to be involved in water conservation in response to desiccation (named ipc-1 and 2a; [Kahsai et al., 2010]), indicating that physiological stress could inform the decision to initiate and sustain courtship via TK signaling.

claim: Courtship in Drosophila consists of a stereotyped sequence of behaviors including orientation, wing vibration, tapping with the forelegs, abdomen curling, and copulation.
source: Courtship in Drosophila consists of a stereotyped sequence of behaviors including orientation, wing vibration, tapping with the forelegs, abdomen curling, and copulation (Spieth, 1974) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript cites Spieth, 1974 as the source for this claim, with Figure 1A providing visual evidence.

claim: The neural circuits underlying olfactory pheromone detection are well described in the silkmoth Bombyx mori.
source: The neural circuits underlying olfactory pheromone detection are well described in the silkmoth Bombyx mori (Sakurai et al., 2014) and honey bee (Roussel et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Sakurai et al., 2014 as the source for this claim.

claim: The neural circuits underlying olfactory pheromone detection are well described in the honey bee.

claim: In Drosophila, the pathways mediating detection of the sex pheromone 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA) have been refined down to 4 neurons connected by 3 synapses.
source: In Drosophila, the pathways mediating detection of the sex pheromone 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA) have been refined down to 4 neurons connected by 3 synapses (Ruta et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ruta et al., 2010 as the source for this claim.

claim: The projection patterns for several olfactory receptor neurons that likely detect sex pheromones have been mapped from the antennal lobe to the ventral lateral horn.
source: In addition, the projection patterns for several other olfactory receptor neurons that likely detect sex pheromones have been mapped from the antennal lobe to the ventral lateral horn, implicating this region in the central brain as a specialized site for processing pheromone odors (Jefferis et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites Jefferis et al., 2007 as the source for this claim.
